newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Bangladesh to shift to cleaner fuels in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh to shift to cleaner fuels in 1997.

text.p: Hot on the heels of India, Bangladesh is also turning green in its use of fuel from next year, official sources said on Tuesday.
An official with state-owned Bangladesh Petroleum Corp (BPC) said it is seeking to import 0.5-percent sulphur diesel and 92-octane unleaded gasoline for January-June 1997 deliveries.
BPC normally buys 1.0-percent sulphur diesel and 80-octane leaded gasoline for domestic use.
In this tender, BPC also seeks 525,000 barrels of 92-octane unleaded gasoline, 560,000 barrels of superior kerosene and 300,000 barrels of aviation jet fuel.
The tender closes on December 3 and offers will be valid until December 18, the official said.
Bangladesh awarded its previous term tender for July-December 1996 deliveries to Petco, the trading arm of Malaysian national oil firm Petronas.

"This is the first time that we are buying 0.5-percent sulphur diesel in large volumes," the official from BPC's commercial division told Reuters by telephone from Dhaka. ""We are doing this for environmental reasons, towards the protection of the environment."
But the official said prices for the better quality material would be an issue and "if it (the price) becomes unbearable on our part, we should rethink."
In a six-month term tender, which was issued recently, BPC seeks about 4.54 million barrels of 0.5-percent sulphur diesel, almost double its previous imports for June-December 1996.

Under the Petco contract, BPC bought 2.03 million barrels of 1.0-percent sulphur diesel, 16 combination cargoes comprising 50,000 barrels of 80-octane leaded gasoline, and 105,000 barrels of diesel, jet fuel and superior kerosene.

India has also shifted to cleaner fuels. It had already lowered diesel sulphur content to 0.5 percent from 1.0 on April this year in the four metropolitan areas of New Delhi, Bombay Calcutta, Madras and the Taj Trapezium in Agra.

Since late July, India has started buying the lower sulphur 0.25 percent grade diesel which was used in the Taj Mahal area since September. This move is to prepare the country for a gradual switch to this grade in most of the countries by 1999 to limit air pollution as the use of diesel-driven vehicles rise.
